subtype: Approach: insisting on copying a friend's grand party [Pitfall]
passage: I'm Rehana, and I live next door to Shankar. On Monday at recess he told everyone about a classmate's party with a magician and a huge bouncy castle. "Mine will be exactly like that," he said. On Tuesday, through the wall, I heard his father say it was too much for the family. Shankar shut his door hard and skipped dinner. On Wednesday he sat on the stairs, staring, and said nothing about the party for two days. Then I saw him drawing on an old calendar page: cricket in the lane, a big chocolate cake, everyone's names. "This is what I actually like," he told me.

qa.q: What did Shankar want at his party?
qa.a: Shankar wanted a bouncy castle and a magician like a classmate's party.

qa.q: What was Shankar feeling after his father said it was too much for the family?
qa.a: Shankar was upset and disappointed; shutting the door hard, skipping dinner and staring silently on the stairs all point to it. 😔

qa.q: What alternative approach could Shankar use, and why?
qa.a: Shankar could start with what he enjoys and what the family can afford, and then add one special touch. A plan that fits the family means less arguing and more fun.

qa.q: How does Rehana see what happens to Shankar?
qa.a: Rehana watches from next door and hears the argument, so Rehana sees a neighbour go from sulking to planning and seems relieved when Shankar shares the drawing.

grounding: A boy insists on copying a classmate's grand party, the family cannot afford it and he is upset until he plans around his own favourites.
